newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Khatami faces difficult economic challenge.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Khatami faces difficult economic challenge.

text.p: President-elect Mohammad Khatami faces a daunting task to revitalise Iran's moribund non-oil economy as a solution to high inflation, unemployment and stagnant exports, Iranian businessmen said on Sunday.

Khatami, whose campaign support included centrist elements close to outgoing President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and reformist technocrats, is expected to follow Iran's current five year economic plan (1995-2000) while emphasising increased investment in the ailing domestic industry.

Lack of industrial investment and output coupled with ailing non-oil exports have helped create annual inflation of 25 percent, unemployment of officially at least 10 percent and a business culture that feeds on Tehran's multi-layered currency rates and patronage rather than productive performance.
Bureaucracy, red tape and unclear tax and investment rules still draw complaints from Iranian and foreign business people alike nearly 10 years after the end of Iran's 1980-1988 war with Iraq.

Khatami, swept to power in a landslide election victory on Saturday, is seen by many local businessmen as the best hope of partly breaking the near-monopolistic power of the bazaaris -- merchants who have historically preferred to make profits out of trading and money-changing rather than industry.

"It was traditionally believed that businessmen were supporters of Nateq-Nouri and it was the young people and women who supported Khatami. But when business isn't working it has to change," said Ali, a local manufacturer.
Iran's conservative Parliamentary Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, unexpectedly defeated by Khatami in the election, had the strong support of the bazaaris, businessman said.

Tehran's rulers have also strongly relied on the country's main asset -- the annual $18 billion in petrodollars which come from being the world's third largest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia and Norway -- to bail the economy out of its troubles.

Exports of Persian carpets and pistachios have contributed to foreign exchange earnings but both these pillars of the non- oil sector have suffered in the past two years since the government introduced tough currency exchange restrictions.
But voices in the business community calling for changes in local industry and commerce are getting louder.
"Industry is bust, privatisation has stalled and there is no proper managerial class," said one industrialist.
Khatami's campaign broadcasts and literature did not amount to an alternative economic programme to the 1995-2000 plan but showed he was at least aware of the problems, businessmen said.

"A priority is to increase industrial exports and ease rules for exporters because our future life and independence relies on non-oil exports," said Khatami, who warned that by 2010 Iran's own oil demand could be so high that its crude production would all be used locally.

Though Iran's oil reserves will last for at least the next 70 years at its current output rate of 3.6 million barrels per day (bpd), the fact that Khatami raised the spectre of an Iran without oil exports showed that he recognised the urgency of boosting local industries, businessmen said.

Washington's reaction to proposed foreign investment in Iran's oil and gas industries will also be crucial to Tehran's plans for securing outside finance to help bolster its petroleum revenue into the next decade.

Khatami has also called for legal changes to encourage non-oil exports, to attract 110 trillion rials ($36.7 billion) of "wandering liquidity" into domestic industry and promised unspecified steps to improve currency stability.

Khatami's attempts to cure the economy will be helped by Rafsanjani's success in controlling a foreign debt which soared above $30 billion in the early 1990s and a growth rate of 4.5 percent in the Iranian year which ended in March.

Rare praise for the country from the International Monetary Fund came last December when IMF officials said Iran had successfully weathered the debt crunch and could look forward to more growth and opening new lines of international credit. ($1=3,000 rials at the official exchange rate)
